## Source Map — GOV-003: Fourth-quarter 2022 public finances and debt

**Document type:** Executive official financial report (press release / communiqué)
**Source role:** Self-presented executive account (SHCP — Treasury Secretariat)
**Reporting period:** Calendar year 2022 (Q4 close), year-end figures; some series to November or October 2022
**Basis:** Not explicitly stated; implied budget-execution (cash or modified cash); coverage unclear — appears to be central federal government only; off-budget entities, state firms, extra-budgetary funds, and pension gaps not addressed

---

### § A — Revenue and budget execution

| ID | Claim | Locator | Verification needed / caveat |
|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | Public revenues in 2022 = 6.595 trillion pesos, 422 billion above programme | Block 4 | Verify against SIG@R budget-execution reports; figure stated net of IEPS subsidy |
| A2 | Revenue growth vs 2021 = +2.5% real annual | Block 4 | Confirm deflator used; base-effect risk |
| A3 | Federal obtained 632 billion pesos above programme; 397 billion from smaller IEPS shortfall than budgeted | Block 4 | Net of subsidy; programme baseline not shown in extract |
| A4 | Petroleum revenues = 1.482 trillion pesos (5.2% of GDP); highest since 2014; +18.7% real YoY vs 2021 | Block 4 | Price-driven; verify against PEMEX financial reports and MoF monthly collections |
| A5 | Tax revenue (ex-IEPS fuel) = 13.6% of GDP; highest on record; +7.8% real YoY vs 2021 | Block 4 | "Combat to tax evasion" cited as driver; verify against SAT annual statistics |
| A6 | ISR (income tax) = 2.270 trillion pesos (8.0% of GDP); record high; +11% YoY; largest since 2016 | Block 4 | Verify against SAT annual return data; real-wage effect cited but not isolated |
| A7 | VAT revenue = 1.222 trillion pesos (4.3% of GDP); above historical average 3.9% | Block 4 | Consumption-driven; verify against customs and SAT VAT reconciliation |
| A8 | Two consecutive years of revenue growth | Block 4 | Confirm 2021 YoY figure independently |

**Qualifications:** No distinction between cash and accrual basis stated. "Presupuestarios" suggests budget-execution basis. Revenue figures are likely gross of refunded taxes / tax credits; whether these are deducted is not specified. GDP denominator — nominal, estimated when? — not clarified.

---

### § B — Public expenditure

| ID | Claim | Locator | Verification needed / caveat |
|---|---|---|---|
| B1 | Public expenditure in 2022 = 7.569 trillion pesos (26.5% of GDP); +4.1% real YoY | Block 5 | Verify SIG@R execution vs approved budget (original vs modified); 3 consecutive years of growth |
| B2 | Social protection spending = 5.3% of GDP (+8.7% real); record high | Block 5 | Scope of "protección social" classification; whether programmes are new or reclassified |
| B3 | Physical investment (inversión física) grew 25.2% real; highest since 2009; = 3.3% of GDP; highest since 2016 | Block 5 | Verify against SFP infrastructure execution reports; includes which entities? |
| B4 | Participations to states/municipalities = record high; +7.3% real annual | Block 5 | Verify against SHCP distribution tables; scope — federal participations only |
| B5 | Public expenditure "oriented to family welfare" | Block 1 | Narrative framing; not a quantified claim |

**Qualifications:** "Gasto del sector público" — if this means *presupuestario*, it likely excludes PEMEX and CFE operational spending and investment. Federal government spending vs public sector (which includes state firms) is not distinguished. Capital investment surge (25.2%) may reflect accelerated disbursement rather than improved project selection.

---

### § C — Fiscal balances and debt

| ID | Claim | Locator | Verification needed / caveat |
|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | Primary balance = −0.5% of GDP | Block 5 | Verify against SHCP monthly balance tables; primary = before interest |
| C2 | Public balance (deficit) = −3.4% of GDP | Block 5 | Slight discrepancy vs primary + interest arithmetic (3.4 − 0.5 = 2.9% of GDP in interest); check rounding, coverage |
| C3 | Public sector financial requirements (RFSP) = 4.4% of GDP | Block 5 | Broader than primary balance; includes SOE financing, contingent liabilities; verify |
| C4 | Fiscal buffers (amortiguadores) = $262 billion combined: international reserves, IMF Flexible Credit Line, Fed swap line, stabilization funds | Block 5 | Verify Balanza de pagos / Banxico reserve data; "swap" as committed vs drawn; stabilization fund composition |
| C5 | Public debt = 49.4% of GDP; 1.6 pp below 2022 programme; 1.4 pp below 2021 | Block 1 | Gross debt; nominal GDP basis; verify vs Banxico / SHCP debt statistics; currency and valuation effects not isolated |
| C6 | "Debt public situated at a sustainable and lower level than 2021" | Block 5 | Self-assessment; no methodology for sustainability provided |
| C7 | For 2023–2025, debt service pressures reduced on average 73%; 2023 administration received $3 billion freed through buybacks | Block 6 | "Promedio" — average of what exactly? Maturity profile of what instruments? $3 billion freed vs what baseline? |
| C8 | 21 international recognitions for debt management strategy over 4 years | Block 6 | Not enumerated; verify against MoF awards record |

---

### § D — Debt operations (2022)

| ID | Claim | Locator | Detail |
|---|---|---|---|
| D1 | 7 Oct 2022: auction of debt *buyback* — 68,017 million pesos; maturities 2023–2046 | Block 6 | Against what outstanding? Which series? |
| D2 | 7 Oct 2022: sale of long-term debt (Bonos/Udibonos) — 48,596 million pesos | Block 6 | New issuance or switch operation? |
| D3 | 30 Nov 2022: 3rd Bondes G issuance — 1yr: 7,090m; 2yr: 2,660m; 3yr: 250m pesos | Block 6 | Short-term instruments; total 10,000m pesos |
| D4 | 7 Dec 2022: new Bono M issued — May 2033; 12,500m pesos; 7.5% coupon | Block 6 | |
| D5 | 8 Dec 2022: Bono M placement — 2033 & 2053 maturities; 50,863m pesos; plus buyback of Bono M 2029–2047 | Block 6 | Net issuance after buyback not specified |

**Qualification:** The document presents each operation but does not net issuance vs refinancing. Some operations appear to be liability-management swaps (same principal, different maturity), which reduce refinancing pressure without changing net debt stock.

---

### § E — Economic indicators (macro context)

| ID | Claim | Locator | Verification needed / caveat |
|---|---|---|---|
| E1 | GDP growth 2.9% to November 2022 | Block 2 | INEGI / Banxico preliminary; partial year; compare with full-year figure |
| E2 | Unemployment rate: 2.8% national, 2.5% women — lowest in 17 years | Block 2 | ENOE survey; 17-year series (2005); verify with INEGI |
| E3 | 2.4 million jobs created in 2022 vs 2021 | Block 2 | Ambiguous source: likely total occupied population (ENO/ENOE), not IMSS |
| E4 | 753,000 new IMSS-registered positions (mainly permanent); 3rd highest since 1997 | Block 3 | INEGI/IMSS data; formal employment only; does NOT reconcile with 2.4m in E3 |
| E5 | Average unemployment 2022 = 3.3% (among lowest on record) | Block 3 | ENOE annual average; reconcile with E2 point-in-time |
| E6 | Average real wage increase = 2.7% annual | Block 3 | ENOE / IMSS; wage bill vs average wage; verify dispersion |
| E7 | IMSS employment in sexenio (Dec 2018–Dec 2022) = 1.3 million net new; higher than Calderón or Fox in same period | Block 3 | Compare with SHCP / IMSS published series |
| E8 | Private consumption +7.1% to Oct 2022; more than double historical average 2.7% | Block 2 | INEGI consumption indicators; partial year; confirm deflator |
| E9 | Gross fixed investment +5.5% to Oct 2022; machinery & equipment +12.2% | Block 3 | INEGI; partial year |
| E10 | Total trade (imports + exports) = $1.2 trillion in 2022; record high | Block 3 | SAT/SE/Banxico; verify |
| E11 | FDI = $32 billion by Q3 2022; highest since 2013 | Block 2 | SE/Banxico; Q4 not yet complete |
| E12 | New FDI investment = second highest after 2013; $14 billion | Block 3 | "Nuevas inversiones" vs total FDI; verify composition |
| E13 | Smaller capital outflows: $19 billion less than 2021 | Block 3 | Banxico/SE; what instrument class? Portfolio vs FDI? |

**Internal inconsistency — critical:** E3 claims 2.4 million jobs created in 2022; E4 records 753,000 IMSS formal positions in 2022. These are not reconcilable as the same metric. The document appears to conflate general employment expansion (ENOE-based) with formal IMSS registrations without flagging the distinction. Both figures appear in the same document.

### § F — Rating and institutional claims

| ID | Claim | Locator | Verification needed / caveat |
|---|---|---|---|
| F1 | Mexico maintains investment grade and stable outlook from all 8 rating agencies | Block 6 | Verify current ratings from each of 8 agencies (Moody's, S&P, Fitch, DBRS, Kroll, Japan Credit Rating, HR Ratings, Verum); confirm no negative watch |
| F2 | Debt positioned to face internal/external shocks | Block 5 | Self-assessment; no stress-test or scenario data cited |

### § G — Narrative / framing items (not verified facts)

| Item | Locator | Issue |
|---|---|---|
| "Finanzas públicas continúan con un manejo responsable" | Block 1 | Institutional self-characterisation; no operationalised criteria |
| "Subsidio al IEPS de combustibles" framed as driver of above-programme revenue | Block 4 | Stimulus reduces revenue vs programme; framed as "additional income" alongside shortfall; conflates two effects |
| "Combate a la evasión fiscal continúa reflejándose positivamente" | Block 4 | Attribution claim; revenue increase attributed entirely to enforcement; ignores macroeconomic and price effects |
| "Blindaje de amortiguadores fiscales" | Block 5 | Narrative; $262 billion combined figure mixes liquid reserves (usable) with committed lines (not necessarily available) |
| "Endeudamiento sostenible y menor al observado en 2021" | Block 5 | Self-assessment; no sustainability methodology cited |
| 73% reduction in debt pressures 2023–2025 | Block 6 | Relative to what baseline? Average of three years? Across which instruments? Not operationalised |
| "Calificaciones…perspectiva estable" | Block 6 | Verbum plenUM; verify each agency individually |

### Score-bearing question coverage (Chapter 5B)

| Question | Coverage in extract |
|---|---|
| **5B.3** Fiscal, tax, debt, monetary rules | Partial: deficit/debt figures given; formal fiscal rule compliance not addressed; RFSP 4.4% cited but no binding rule reference |
| **5B.7** Reliability of economic information, auditability | Weak: data are self-reported by SHCP; no independent audit cited; methodology/definitions not specified; discrepancies between employment metrics not flagged |
| **5B.9** Response to shocks, funding, targeting | Partial: buffers listed ($262bn); fiscal stimulus not discussed as explicit shock response; no programme-level targeting assessment |
| **5B.10** Trajectory — stronger/more durable | Not assessed: forward-looking narrative; no independent sustainability analysis; debt-reduction attributed to own operations without third-party corroboration |
| 5B.1 Public goods / service delivery | Not addressed: investment and social spending growth cited, but delivery efficiency and coverage not assessed |
| 5B.6 Rule of law / property rights | Not addressed |
| 5B.8 Regulatory / business environment | Not addressed |
| 5B.5 Social welfare / poverty reduction | Not addressed: social spending growth stated; poverty/outcome data absent |

---

### Observed limitations and reopeners

1. **Employment metric discrepancy (critical):** 2.4 million total jobs (ENOE) vs 753,000 formal IMSS registrations in the same 2022 period. Document treats these as complementary without acknowledging the distinction. A stronger model should require reconciliation or clarification from SHCP/INEGI.
2. **IEPS fuel subsidy framing:** The 397 billion peso "revenue gain" from lower-than-budgeted IEPS subsidy is presented alongside the 632 billion peso above-programme total, creating an ambiguity — are both figures additive vs offsetting? The document should specify the programme baseline for each.
3. **GDP denominator:** 49.4% debt-to-GDP uses nominal GDP; currency appreciation/depreciation and GDP revisions affect this figure independently of policy. No adjustment or sensitivity stated.
4. **Debt buffer composition:** $262 billion "blindaje" mixes liquid reserves (immediately available) with committed but undrawn facilities (IMF, Fed swap), which are not fungible in a crisis. Composition not disaggregated.
5. **73% debt pressure reduction:** The metric is unexplained — average reduction across which years, which instruments, relative to which baseline? Should be verified against SHCP debt maturity schedule.
6. **Net new borrowing vs refinancing:** Debt operations are presented without net-issuance figures; it is unclear whether 2022 reduced the debt stock or merely extended maturities.
7. **Formal vs informal employment framing:** The 2.4 million job figure is used for headline employment performance while IMSS formal registrations (753,000) are cited for structural quality; both appear without acknowledging the gap.
8. **Revenue attribution:** Increases in ISR and VAT are attributed to enforcement and real-wage growth without isolating inflation effects (which inflate nominal revenue without real increase) or commodity-price base effects on oil revenues.
9. **Sustainability narrative unaccompanied:** The claim of debt sustainability and trajectory improvement is not supported by any model, stress test, or independent assessment in the extract.

---

**Source-map integrity check:** All 34 numbered claims above have a locator reference within blocks 1–6 of the extract. No locator is absent. No claim has been invented beyond the text in the extract. Four claims (E3/E4 conflict, C2 arithmetic, C7 unverified) are flagged as reopeners requiring additional evidence.
